items.explanation: L1 distinguishes these as genuinely different claims — one about available room given existing commitments, the other about ability — a bare 'no' doesn't distinguish them.

Capability

Ability to do the work at all

items.prompt: What is "sustainable boundary-setting" as this unit defines it?
choices: The practice of surfacing capacity limits as they're reached, so workload decisions get made deliberately instead of by default through silent overextension
The practice of refusing all new work requests outright, applied as a fixed, blanket policy regardless of context
A formal HR process that requires filing a written workload complaint before any new request can be declined
The practice of only ever working the exact hours listed in an employment contract, with no flexibility at all
items.explanation: Sustainable boundary-setting is specifically about deliberate, visible trade-off decisions — not blanket refusal, HR processes, or rigid hour-counting.
items.reference:
👁️ Make the capacity limit visible and factual
🤝 Put the trade-off decision in the requester's hands

Why: the goal isn't refusing work — it's making sure new work gets added with an explicit, deliberate trade-off.
items.learnMore:
What it is, and isn't
IsIsn't
GoalDeliberate, visible trade-off decisionsAvoiding all new work

Treating boundary-setting as one dramatic refusal rather than an ongoing habit of surfacing limits every time they're actually reached.

A performance review metric that a manager tracks privately, without the employee ever seeing or discussing it
items.explanation: A capacity signal is specifically a factual, contextual statement — not an HR filing, a vague complaint, or a formal metric.
items.reference:

"I'm pretty busy"

Capacity signal

Why: a credible signal names specific commitments and deadlines — context, not an excuse.

items.prompt: What is "trade-off framing"?
choices: Presenting a new request alongside its real cost, rather than giving a flat yes or no
A negotiation tactic used exclusively in formal salary and compensation discussions, not everyday workload requests
A framework used for evaluating a company's overall business strategy at the leadership and board level
A method for splitting credit fairly between multiple team members who contributed to a shared project
items.explanation: Trade-off framing is specifically about surfacing the real cost of saying yes — not salary negotiation, business strategy, or credit-splitting.
items.reference:
① State the capacity signal
↓
② Offer the trade-off, not a flat answer
↓
③ Requester decides, with the real cost visible

Why: a flat yes or no skips the step where the real cost gets seen by the person who can actually weigh it.
items.learnMore:
Trade-off framing, laid out
New request arrives
↓
State current commitments (the capacity signal)
↓
Offer the trade-off: "I can take this on if X moves, or decline and keep X on track"
↓
Requester decides, with the real cost visible

The requester gets the decision because they usually hold the context — relative urgency — that the person raising the constraint doesn't.

Common mistake

Deciding unilaterally which existing commitment should slip, then only informing the requester afterward. That skips the one step — their actual say — that makes this fair.
